item.title: Trump’s FCC pick advances despite Democratic boycott
item.description: Democratic Senate Commerce Committee members skipped the vote in an attempt to protest Danielle Thumann Severs’ nomination.

media:content.media:title: The Senate Commerce Committee leaders have been at odds over advancing President Donald Trump's FCC nominee.

item.dc:creator: By John Hendel
item.content:encoded:
Senate Commerce Committee Republicans on Wednesday advanced President Donald Trump’s pick to fill an open Federal Communications Commission seat despite a Democratic boycott meant to obstruct the session.

The vote boosts the likelihood that Republicans confirm Danielle Thumann Severs in the lame duck while the party still controls the chamber. That confirmation would cement a deeper Republican majority at the telecom regulator and reduce the need for Trump to compromise and nominate Democrats next year.

Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz (R-Texas) called Democrats’ “temper tantrum” Wednesday a “terrible harbinger” heading into the new Congress.

Democrats view the nomination vote as a broader fight for the future of the five-member FCC, which typically is supposed to have members from both parties. But Democrats fear Trump could fire Anna Gomez, the lone Democrat, if he is able to add Thumann Severs to the FCC since it would still have a quorum.

“All Democratic members of the Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee object to the majority stacking independent commissions with Republicans and rushing nominees through the Committee process in this lame duck session with no Democratic pairs,” Senate Commerce ranking member Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) said in a statement before the 10 a.m. scheduled start time.

FCC Chair Brendan Carr currently holds a 2-1 GOP majority, and he requires at least three members for a quorum to conduct much of the FCC's business.

“We made clear to Chairman Cruz that we had concerns about the nominee for the Federal Communications Commission being on the Executive Session until a Democratic nominee is put forward and asked that she be pulled from the markup,” Cantwell added. “Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times. This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.”

Cruz said the administration has recently made clear it will move Democratic nominees and maintained Republicans are still in the right to move nominations before them now.

Democrats also worry that Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to Carr, won’t be an independent voice on the commission. Carr has faced particularly intense criticism for how he has threatened and investigated media companies, including this year threatening the eight ABC station licenses of Disney and his scrutiny of TV hosts like Jimmy Kimmel.

item.title: Democrats overwhelmingly nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker
item.description: He received an overwhelming, but not unanimous, endorsement from the incoming majority.

media:content.media:title: House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries speaks during a press conference on Capitol Hill on Nov. 17, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York secured his fellow Democrats’ nomination Wednesday to lead the House, putting him on track to be elected the first Black speaker in January.

Jeffries, who has served in the House since 2013 and as minority leader since 2023, won the uncontested secret ballot 251-11 — an overwhelming, but not unanimous, endorsement from the incoming majority.

While some incoming members withheld their support, he chipped away at skeptics in private meetings and public policy commitments. His candidacy was buoyed by Democrats’ massive midterm victories that delivered a majority that could reach 260 seats once all votes are counted.

Several lawmakers representing different wings of the caucus spoke in favor of Jeffries before the vote, including progressive Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández of New Mexico, Rep.-elect Rebecca Bennett from a Wisconsin swing district and Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina — previously the highest-ranking Black House Democrat before Jeffries’ ascension.

In his pitch to members, Jeffries, 56, leaned heavily on his record during two terms as party leader, highlighting Democrats’ resolve during shutdown fights and their success cornering Republicans through procedural maneuvers.

Progressives are enthused that Jeffries this week embraced lowering the Medicare eligibility age, expanding coverage to include vision, dental and hearing benefits, as well as establishing universal health coverage for children. Centrists have long backed Jeffries, cheering him as a pragmatic, consensus-oriented leader.

Some of the 11 holdouts issued a joint statement Wednesday acknowledging ongoing "good-faith conversations" with Jeffries but adding "there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership."

The group of seven incoming members includes several self-identified democratic socialists, including Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, Melat Kiros of Colorado and Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania.

“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues," they said.

Jeffries has previewed that early votes under his leadership will include ending President Donald Trump’s tariffs, clawing back Republican-led Medicaid cuts and restoring expired Affordable Care Act tax credits.

He has also emphasized an oversight agenda that targets Trump, his administration and his allies, as well as anti-corruption measures such as a congressional stock trading ban.

item.title: Ted Lieu is elected House Democratic Caucus chair
item.description: He is set to be the highest-ranking Asian American House member ever.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) speaks while Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries watches during a press conference in Washington on Nov. 4, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Ted Lieu of California was elected House Democratic Caucus chair Wednesday morning in a closed-door meeting — the first of numerous leadership elections set to be decided this week.

Lieu, 57, won by acclamation in an uncontested bid for the post, meaning no official vote was tallied. He moves up from caucus vice chair and is now positioned to be the highest-ranking Asian American House member ever.

House Democrats will vote next on a nomination for speaker, where Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is uncontested, followed by elections for majority leader, whip and numerous junior caucus positions.

item.title: Bipartisan Senate duo urges ‘immediate’ White House action on AI-enabled cyber threats
item.description: Sens. Maria Cantwell and Mike Rounds want leaders to harness existing federal agencies to counter major disruptions.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) arrives for a vote at the U.S. Capitol on June 8, 2026. (Francis Chung/POLITICO via AP Images)

item.dc:creator: By Kelsey Brugger
item.content:encoded:
Sens. Maria Cantwell and Mike Rounds called on the White House Tuesday night to “take immediate action” to protect against intensifying artificial-intelligence-juiced cyber threats against the nation’s infrastructure, financial institutions and software.

The bipartisan duo sent a letter to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, chair of the recently formed “Superintelligence Task Force,” urging him to quickly bring together developers and federal experts to fully use the administration’s tools to counter cyber attacks plaguing banks and other systems.

“AI is rapidly increasing the ability to discover and exploit weaknesses in software, and our defenses are not keeping pace,” wrote Cantwell of Washington, the top Democrat on Senate Commerce Committee, and Rounds of South Dakota, the chair of the Armed Services cybersecurity subcommittee. “We cannot meet these threats with yesterday's cybersecurity infrastructure or rely on individual companies to solve a problem that spans the entire digital economy.”

A spokesperson for Clayton did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The new letter comes as the world faces credible threats of AI-enabled hacking targeting bank accounts and highly trafficked websites, jeopardizing personal and financial information worldwide.

Members of Congress are trying to figure out what to do about it, and the senators want Trump administration officials to use existing federal agencies and departments to fend off harm from models going rogue.

The letter urges the White House to direct the National Institute of Standards and Technology to craft security standards for defensive AI agents and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to accelerate their adoption at banks, hospitals, utilities and government agencies.

The senators said the expertise within the federal government exists but that a coordinated approach is absent.

“The United States has the technological expertise to lead this effort,” the senators wrote. “What is missing is a coordinated national strategy to bring these capabilities together, establish common security standards, and put effective defenses into widespread use.”

As likely Commerce chair next year, Cantwell will have a new perch to push the administration and conduct oversight as she sees fit. Last month, she released a comprehensive framework that aims to tackle catastrophic risk and other problems.

item.title: Garcia gives Trump allies early warning on the investigations to come
item.description: Democrats plan to use their new power to investigate the White House’s role in the release of the Jeffrey Epstein files and Trump family business dealings.

media:content.media:title: House Oversight Committee Ranking Member Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) departs a vote at the U.S. Capitol on June 23, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Kyle Cheney and Chris Marquette
item.dc:contributor: By Kyle Cheney and Chris Marquette
item.content:encoded:
House Democrats are signaling their top investigative targets in the new Congress, starting with President Donald Trump’s family members and closest aides — from sons Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump to chief of staff Stephen Miller, former chief Susie Wiles and Vice President JD Vance.

Rep. Robert Garcia, who is expected to be the next chair of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, sent letters to all five Wednesday morning, indicating they will be subjects of interest to the panel next year as he prepares to make good on his promise to probe Trump family business ties, ICE’s mass deportation campaign, the administration’s handling of the Epstein files and more.

The California Democrat sent a total of 12 letters to high-profile figures in Trump’s orbit, including Trump son-in-law Jared Kushner, Attorney General Todd Blanche and former ambassador Kimberly Guilfoyle, as well as former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and her former adviser Corey Lewandowski. The letters, which have no legal force, urge the recipients to preserve documents in anticipation of the investigations Democrats plan to launch when they take over the House in January. And they provide the clearest early window into the soon-to-be-majority’s most pressing investigative priorities.

It’s a sign the incoming Democratic majority will not shy away from confrontations with the White House that could lead to court battles likely to drag on for the remainder of Trump’s term. Administrations of both parties have typically treated senior White House officials — especially chiefs of staff like Miller and Wiles — as immune from compelled testimony to Congress.

The letters are an answer to the Trump administration’s recent warnings about potential criminal prosecution of Democrats who engage in oversight activities it considers “weaponized” or overly punitive.

The White House and Justice Department also have repeatedly warned of possible criminal investigations for demands they consider out of bounds — or lacking a “legitimate legislative task,” as longstanding precedents require. Garcia’s 12 letters nod to that requirement, each including a line describing the investigations as “essential for legislative reform.”

“As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans,” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said. “If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people.”

The Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Though some letters request responses by December, Democrats don’t yet have the power to compel answers. And even when they do, congressional oversight requests — including subpoena deadlines — are typically flexible and depend on the targets’ willingness to negotiate and cooperate.

Here’s what Oversight Committee Democrats are most interested in pursuing come January:

Trump family business dealings

Garcia is signaling that Donald Trump Jr. and his brother Eric Trump will be the subjects of an inquiry into their roles as co-founders of World Liberty Financial, a Trump family cryptocurrency business. The committee’s top Democrat describes the brothers as key players in “the Trump family’s pay-to-play schemes” which “have raked in billions of dollars for the Trump family over the past several years.” A World Liberty Financial spokesperson has previously said “no one at World Liberty Financial works for the U.S. Government” and the company is compliant with all U.S. laws.

Donald Trump Jr. is also under scrutiny in connection with his elaborate wedding celebration that was funded by Umar Kremlev, a Russian oligarch with ties to President Vladimir Putin. Kremlev has said the younger Trump paid him back. Donald Trump Jr. and his wife Bettina Trump wrote in a social media post that the celebration was an “extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend” that had been “recast as something political or sinister.”

“Foreign interests also funded your lavish wedding celebrations, raising further concerns of pay-to-play schemes and foreign intelligence infiltration of the Trump family,” Garcia said. “These associations may have already benefited special interests, but they have not helped the American people.”

Democrats also have their sights on Kushner, the president’s son-in-law and a U.S. special envoy, for his personal business dealings and government work. Garcia raised concerns that “hundreds of millions of dollars in management fees, business opportunities, and other financial benefits are serving as disguised payoffs for policy changes, preferential treatment, relief from legal scrutiny, and access to sensitive government information and technology.” Kushner has repeatedly denied leveraging his powerful father-in-law for personal gain.

"These allegations have it exactly backwards. Jared Kushner has always acted in the best interests of the United States,” Chad Mizelle, Kushner’s attorney, said. “He has voluntarily stepped away from his successful business to devote his time, without compensation, to helping President Trump end wars, save lives, and advance American interests. Any suggestion that he has used his public service for personal financial gain is categorically false."

The White House has repeatedly denied that Trump or his family members have engaged in any conflicts of interest. The Trump brothers did not immediately return requests for comment.

Garcia also wrote to Catherine Townsend, CEO of the Trust for the National Mall, inquiring about donations by private entities and companies to support Trump’s White House ballroom. Among the companies named is the embattled chip manufacturer Nvidia, which Garcia notes “donated millions to the Trust for the National Mall shortly after receiving permission from the Trump Administration to sell advanced microchips to the People’s Republic of China.”

Nvidia has maintained its donation was made independently of any potential business interests. Townsend was not immediately reachable for comment.

Immigration enforcement

Garcia also outlined the panel’s plans to investigate “the violence, abuse, and corruption carried out by the Department of Homeland Security” under Miller’s direction. The committee said it has found 1,165 instances of concerning uses of force, arrests, deportations and enforcement actions at sensitive locations and other “acts of intimidation or retaliation.”

“Members of the Trump Administration have described you as the ‘linchpin’ and ‘architect’ of the Trump Administration’s most extreme policies, advocating for the widespread abuse of civil liberties,” Garcia wrote to Miller, now Trump’s chief of staff. “We have documented, and will continue to document, your role in orchestrating, overseeing, and defending these abuses.”

Garcia also pledged to investigate allegations that Noem “abused DHS funds, undermined career employees, circumvented established safeguards that prevent corruption, and used your position to enrich yourself and associates of the Trump Administration.”

The letter to Noem also makes note of her role running an agency that presided over “pay-to-play schemes conducted” by Lewandowski, her former employee at DHS who is also being probed by the committee for alleged kickbacks from GEO Group, a company that runs private detention facilities for migrants. Lewandowski has previously denied demanding payments from the company.

“Congressman Garcia’s attempts to build a misleading narrative about Mr. Lewandowski as part of his party’s campaign against the current administration will be proven false at the appropriate time and in the appropriate forum,” a spokesperson for Lewandowski said.

Noem was forced out of DHS in March after facing intense scrutiny inside the White House and calls from some GOP lawmakers to resign over her management of the department.

Noem did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Epstein files

Garcia is also probing the administration’s handling of the investigative materials related to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and the web of people and institutions who allegedly aided his crimes.

In a letter to Vance, Garcia asked the vice president to identify every meeting officials had on the Epstein files, citing reports outlining Vance’s role in the conversations. Garcia is also seeking information related to the administration’s response to the law Congress passed last year mandating the files’ public disclosure, which lawmakers in both parties have panned as incomplete.

Justice Department officials have said they did their best to follow the law’s disclosure requirements and have sought to correct any errors or address victims’ concerns, but Democrats are still clamoring for sworn testimony from Blanche, who had a key role in overseeing the files’ release.

Garcia is also demanding information about the decision to move Ghislaine Maxwell, Epstein's co-conspirator, to a lower security federal prison where she’s serving a 20-year sentence.

He wrote to Federal Bureau of Prisons Director William Marshall III as well as to Tanisha Hall — the warden of Federal Prison Camp Bryan who runs the minimum security facility where Maxwell was moved — to get answers about Maxwell’s transfer after the Justice Department and the Bureau of Prisons “failed to meaningfully respond to any of our inquiries.”

Marshall and Hall did not immediately return requests for comment.

Garcia is, in addition, asking Wiles — Trump’s former chief of staff — and Blanche for information related to the Epstein saga. Wiles was also unreachable for comment.

Riley Rogerson contributed to this report.

item.title: US to reach $41T debt limit in February or March, forecasters predict
item.description: Reaching the borrowing cap will put an urgent to-do item on the agenda of the new Democrat-run Congress.

media:content.media:title: Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent speaks during the midterm convention.

item.dc:creator: By Jennifer Scholtes
item.content:encoded:
The United States is forecast to reach the $41.1 trillion debt limit in February or March, spurring a high-stakes fiscal policy debate during the early days of the Democrat-controlled Congress.

The Bipartisan Policy Center released that updated projection Wednesday, predicting that the federal government could get by for another six to nine months thereafter, since Treasury can deploy its usual cash-conservation tactics — known as “extraordinary measures” — once the debt limit is reached.

That means Congress’ drop-dead deadline for preventing a debt default, called the X-date, could fall sometime between August and December of next year.

The independent think tank, respected on Capitol Hill for its accurate forecasting of the debt limit in years past, noted that U.S. debt has risen faster than projected since last year, in part because the Trump administration is raking in less cash than expected from tariffs.

Democratic lawmakers have already started discussing the possibility of raising the debt limit through the party-line reconciliation process, like their GOP counterparts did last year.

That would spare the new majority party from having to strike up bipartisan negotiations with President Donald Trump and Republican lawmakers, under pressure from fiscal conservatives to demand spending limits as a condition of allowing the nation to take on more red ink.

item.title: Democrats on House Judiciary and Foreign Affairs probing Lutnick family’s role in Nvidia scandal
item.description: Reps. Jamie Raskin and Greg Meeks are also investigating the Commerce Secretary’s old firm, Cantor Fitzgerald.

media:content.media:title: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick arrives for an American mining industry roundtable at State Department headquarters in Washington, D.C. on Aug. 7, 2026. (Francis Chung/POLITICO via AP Images)

item.dc:creator: By Chris Marquette
item.content:encoded:
Democrats on the House Judiciary and Foreign Affairs Committees are launching a probe into whether the Trump administration’s response to Nvidia’s alleged chip smuggling into Beijing was influenced by the significant shares that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s family holds in the company.

It comes amid the larger fallout from allegations that Nvidia’s ex-CEO, Jensen Huang, had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who was, in turn, accused of funneling advanced chips to China through the firm Megaspeed. It also provides a window into how the incoming chairs of Judiciary and Foreign Affairs — Reps. Jamie Raskin of Maryland and Gregory Meeks of New York, respectively — plan to leverage their new majority in January to advance existing lines of inquiry into this episode.

That includes shining a spotlight on Lutnick, who is also coming under scrutiny for appearing too close to Huang and not doing enough to crack down on Nvidia’s chip sales to China — including by leaving Megaspeed off a list of companies deemed national security risks.

Raskin, Meeks and Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-Calif.), another signatory on the letter, want to know whether there’s any connection between those accusations against Lutnick and the fact that he previously held more than $1.3 billion in Nvidia stock through the investment firm Cantor Fitzgerald, which he ran until he transferred ownership to his children at the time of his confirmation in 2025.

“If these media reports are accurate, the American people deserve to know: Did the Secretary of Commerce seriously and perhaps irreversibly compromise U.S. national security interests to make money for his adult children and Cantor Fitzgerald?” Raskin and Meeks said in a letter dated Nov. 17 to Brandon Lutnick, who is currently serving as the firm’s chair.

“Secretary Lutnick’s reported obstruction may have resulted in billions of dollars of restricted AI chips being diverted to China,” the lawmakers continued. “It also propped up the prices of NVIDIA for months, preventing devastating losses for your company, which not only held a substantial position in NVIDIA, but strongly encouraged its clients to buy NVIDIA stock.”

Meeks, Raskin and Kamlager-Dove told Brandon Lutnick they want all communications with Cantor Fitzgerald clients referring to U.S. export control changes on advanced semiconductors, including with respect to Nvidia customers like Megaspeed. They’re also asking for all information concerning personal investments or other financial interests in Nvidia by Howard Lutnick and President Donald Trump along with documents showing every trade involving Nvidia stock executed by Cantor Fitzgerald between Jan. 1, 2024 to the present.

“Failure to preserve relevant materials could impede congressional oversight and any subsequent investigation. We therefore request written confirmation by 5:00 p.m. on December 1, 2026, that Cantor Fitzgerald has implemented appropriate preservation measures and instructed all relevant personnel to retain potentially responsive records,” the lawmakers wrote.


Danielle Popper, a spokesperson for Cantor Fitzgerald, called the claims made by the letter “inaccurate” and maintained the firm is “in full compliance with all applicable rules and regulations.”

“Cantor holds no material proprietary position in Nvidia,” Popper said in a statement. “Cantor’s Nvidia holdings arise primarily from equity swaps executed for clients. We buy the underlying shares to hedge those trades. The decline in our holdings since early 2025 reflects the unwinding of those hedges as clients closed or reduced their swap positions, not a Cantor decision to exit a proprietary position.”

She added that “allegations suggesting that work influenced government decisions are baseless” and that “Cantor has no role in U.S. export control or Entity List decisions.”

A spokesperson for the Commerce Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

While Democrats have no means or authority to compel the release of this information now, they are laying the groundwork for early next year, when Raskin and Meeks will have the ability to deploy subpoenas to access certain information and force people to testify.

item.title: ‘Looks a lot different now’: Black Democrats are no longer in lockstep on seniority
item.description: Divisions on committee term limits come at a moment of triumph for the powerful Congressional Black Caucus.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Jahana Hayes (D-Conn.) is challenging a fellow CBC member for the Education and Labor gavel.

item.dc:creator: By Riley Rogerson and Mackenzie Wilkes
item.dc:contributor: By Riley Rogerson and Mackenzie Wilkes
item.content:encoded:
The Congressional Black Caucus has long served as the top champion for House Democrats’ strict seniority system, beating back multiple attempts to encourage turnover in the top party echelon.

Now the calls for generational change inside the party are coming from within its own ranks.

Several long-tenured Black committee leaders are looking to get their gavels back when Democrats retake the majority in January. They include Rep. Bennie Thompson of Mississippi, who is 78; Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia, who is 79; and Rep. Maxine Waters of California, who is 88. All have served at least a decade atop their respective committees — Homeland Security, Education and Workforce, and Financial Services.

But many newer and some senior members are saying they’re open to supporting term limits, defying a longstanding CBC position in favor of seniority that defenders say has been the cornerstone of Black power on Capitol Hill. Multiple committee leaders are facing insurgent challengers, with Scott staring down a contest with a fellow CBC member, Rep. Jahana Hayes of Connecticut.

“Debate is always a good thing,” Rep. Shomari Figures of Alabama said in an interview, acknowledging the difference of opinions in the caucus. “CBC looks a lot different now than it did 10 years ago, let alone 20 or 30 years ago.”

The newly emerging divisions inside the CBC on the term-limits issue come at a moment of triumph for the powerful caucus. Its ranks will swell to more than 60 members next year after Black candidates defied Republican attempts to eliminate minority-majority districts with mid-cycle redistricting.

The debate is expected to play out over the next two weeks ahead of a caucus rules vote in early December. Rep. Susie Lee of Nevada is proposing to establish a four-term limit on committee leadership, which would force Scott, Thompson and Waters out of their posts after the coming Congress unless they seek a waiver. The same would be true for Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York, who leads Democrats on Foreign Affairs.

The evolving perspectives inside the CBC are one reason, many observers say, that a Democratic term limits proposal could actually be adopted this year. Republicans have had a three-term limit for their committee leaders in place for more than 30 years, though waivers have been granted in some circumstances allowing members to serve longer.

Meeks, a former CBC chair, and Rep. Yvette Clarke of New York, the current chair, oppose committee term limits, evoking well-known and previously effective arguments that minority members can find it harder to pull key levers of internal power — such as fundraising — and that seniority is an effective equalizer.

“I think the voters make the determination on term limits,” Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina said in an interview. “I think that we have to protect seniority in this place.”

Clyburn, for years the highest-ranking Black leader in Congress, has also noted in the past that Black lawmakers of his generation had to work harder to get elected to office, meaning they often started later in their careers than their white counterparts.

But that seniority principle no longer enjoys near-universal agreement in the caucus ranks. In a sign of the sea change, CBC member and presumptive speaker Hakeem Jeffries is letting the term-limits debate play out, last week calling it “the right conversation to have.”

“Like anything else, members of the CBC have different ideas,” said Rep. Troy Carter of Louisiana, who is running unopposed to lead the caucus next year. “We're not a monolith, and we encourage people to have their own thoughts and ideas.”

For all the clout it affords the most veteran Democrats, the seniority system can seem daunting to younger members who face the prospect of having to serve a decade or more before winning a gavel on a choice committee. And some new and existing CBC members are speaking out.

“I think it should be considered,” Rep.-elect La Shawn Ford of Illinois said in an interview about term limits for committee leaders. “You do want experienced people on leading committees, but I don't think that it should be the only factor that determines a chair vote.”

The internal debate has been dramatically underscored by Hayes’ run against Scott for the top job on the Education and Workforce Committee, which is likely to be renamed Education and Labor under Democratic control.

“I understand why CBC had long-held positions because things had not been fair for a very long time,” Hayes said in an interview. But, she added, “the caucus is getting bigger and bigger, and people come with different backgrounds and different perspectives.“

Clarke said the CBC is unlikely to wade into the Hayes vs. Scott race, explaining that the caucus doesn’t typically endorse in committee chair contests. (Rep. Suzanne Bonamici of Oregon, who is not a member of the CBC, is also running for the Education gavel and has vowed to serve no more than four years).

But last month, Clarke issued a statement of support for Waters, who is seeking an eighth term leading Democrats on the Financial Services Committee against a bid from Rep. Sean Casten of Illinois. She said the CBC is “unwavering in its support” of the longtime leader.

At least one CBC member, Rep. Shontel Brown of Ohio, is running for a vacant role atop the Agriculture Committee against the more senior Rep. Jim Costa of California. A second, Rep. Don Davis of North Carolina, has talked to colleagues about running.

While the debate is breaking down on perhaps predictable generational lines, there are some complications to that narrative.

Rep.-elect Melat Kiros of Colorado said in an interview she is supporting Waters’ bid to remain atop the Financial Services panel past her 90th birthday, while also saying “term limits are important so that we can start building the bench.”

“I think term limits are important, and I think it's also important that we make sure that we're still seeing representation on a lot of these different committees,” she said.

Some longtime members, meanwhile, are at least open to a debate.

Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman of New Jersey is retiring after 12 years in the House. Much of that she spent on the Appropriations Committee, where she never even led a subcommittee. (She did chair a Homeland Security subcommittee at one point.)

“I see both sides — I really see the value of institutional knowledge and experience,” she said, pointing to Thompson’s service atop Homeland Security and the Jan. 6 select committee.

But she pointed to two younger members — Reps. Jamie Raskin of Maryland and Robert Garcia of California — who beat out more seasoned members to take over the Judiciary and Oversight panels, respectively.

“It kind of works out sometimes,” she said.

item.title: Murkowski faces real challenge in bid to be top GOP appropriator
item.description: Two GOP senators predicted Republicans on the committee would support Sen. Jerry Moran, who is challenging her for the position.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Lisa Murkowski arrives for a vote at the U.S. Capitol on March 20.

item.dc:creator: By Jordain Carney, Katherine Tully-McManus and Jennifer Scholtes
item.dc:contributor: By Jordain Carney, Katherine Tully-McManus and Jennifer Scholtes
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Lisa Murkowski is facing a serious challenge in her bid to lead Republicans on the Appropriations Committee next year.

Many expected it to be a foregone conclusion that the Alaska lawmaker would succeed outgoing chair Susan Collins of Maine, who lost her reelection earlier this month; Murkowski is currently the most senior member of the GOP side of the committee dais eligible for a promotion.

But two Republican senators, granted anonymity to speak candidly, said they currently expect GOP members of the Senate Appropriations Committee to instead pick Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kansas) as the party’s vice-chair.

“Moran will win,” said one of the senators in an interview Tuesday regarding the anticipated outcome of the committee vote.

Republicans on the Appropriations Committee won’t have the final say — and it’s still early in the discussions about who will get top Senate committee slots. But opting to effectively bless leapfrogging Murkowski in favor of Moran would be an astounding move for a conference that has long relied on seniority to determine who gets to lead the GOP on committees.

Republican appropriators will vote in January, once new GOP senators are added to the panel, for who they want leading them on the committee. That is, however, only a recommendation that has to then be upheld by the full Senate Republican Conference.

And it’s not clear, currently, how the full Senate GOP conference would handle a recommendation to set aside Murkowski as the top Republican on the panel, according to the two Senate Republicans as well as an additional GOP senator and two aides with knowledge of the matter — also granted anonymity to speak candidly given the sensitivity of the race.

The third senator said they weren’t yet sure who would win the vote among Appropriations Committee Republicans, but that they had advised Moran to “touch base with his leadership team … because the implications to losing a chairmanship also means bigger things for the conference.”

The ramifications, some Republicans worry, could involve a scenario where more GOP senators feel empowered to challenge more senior members for committee leadership spots, prompting open warfare as the party is still trying to regroup after a bruising election cycle. It would also just mark a deviation from the way the conference typically does business — though the conference rules don’t require that the top spot for a committee also be the most senior member.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune said last week he hadn’t yet weighed into the dispute between Murkowski and Moran but that he had advised them to “talk it out” and that “we’ll see where those conversations lead.”

Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), a member of leadership and a high-ranking appropriator, said Tuesday she didn’t know what the outcome of the contest would be but that Murkowski and Moran will meet this week.

Murkowski and Moran have in the meantime both been privately meeting with, and making the case to, colleagues. Spokespeople for neither of the two GOP senators provided a request for comment Tuesday.

Moran did not articulate to POLITICO last week a reason for why he would challenge Murkowski. She will, however, be the most moderate GOP senator remaining come January, and has broken with her party on numerous high-profile decisions over the years.

Democrats also view Murkowski as someone they could potentially negotiate with on government spending deals but are staying out of the GOP dispute.

“Boy, that’s an [intra]party fight on that side. You know, I would have to say on our side that would be really hard, where somebody who’s done all the work and moved their way up — but that’s their neighborhood,” Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.), who will chair the committee next year, said in an interview.

Also potentially working to Murkowski’s disadvantage is that Republicans will be losing five senators on the Appropriations Committee come January, many of whom would have likely been Murkowski allies. It’s not yet clear who will get their spots and who Murkowski and Moran will need to win over.

And even as Republicans grapple with Murkowski’s fate, they appear poised to let GOP senators who have infuriated their colleagues over the past year hold top committee spots. Sens. Mike Lee of Utah and Rand Paul of Kentucky — two notorious thorns in leadership’s side — are, respectively, on tap to be ranking members on the Judiciary Committee and the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions panel.

Neither man currently has a challenger seeking to bypass the seniority system.

item.title: House Ethics responds to calls for sexual misconduct rules changes
item.description: The panel will hold a public meeting Thursday to approve new rules for how it investigates misconduct allegations.

media:content.media:title: House Ethics Committee Chair Michael Guest (R-Miss.) and Ranking Member Mark DeSaulnier (D-Calif.) prepare to convene a hearing originally scheduled to consider sanctions against former Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick (D-Fla.) on Capitol Hill on April 21, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Chris Marquette
item.content:encoded:
The House Ethics Committee will convene a rare public meeting Thursday to consider changes to its own internal rules for handling sexual misconduct allegations — and scale back requirements for issuing subpoenas during its investigations.

It comes as the panel has been pushed to reexamine its practices amid a wave of sexual misconduct allegations among members of both parties, inspiring a bipartisan effort to standardize how these allegations are addressed in order to hold lawmakers more accountable for their actions.

“The Committee has undertaken a review of the rules with the goal of improving the speed of investigations and increasing transparency, particularly with respect to allegations of sexual misconduct,” reads a press release accompanying the meeting notice.

“While the Committee has identified areas for improvement,” the statement continued, “the Committee also seeks to preserve the procedures that ensure fairness, due process, and bipartisanship in all investigations.”

The Ethics Committee, which operates largely in secret, will vote Thursday on whether to formalize, through a rule, a longstanding practice to publicly disclose when a member is found to have engaged in sexual harassment or other sexual misconduct violations — as long as the victim's identity is kept hidden.

It will consider whether to allow only the top Republican and Democrat to sign off on issuing a subpoena, bypassing the need to hold a full committee vote with the hope of expediting the investigative process.

Another change being debated would require any Ethics subcommittee investigating a matter to conclude its work once it adopts its findings, enabling the full committee to then more quickly make a determination on how best to proceed.

The committee could adopt these rules changes, and others, as Reps. Kat Cammack (R-Fla.) and Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.) continue to fine-tune legislation that would make sweeping changes to how the full House polices bad behavior in the rank and file.

Their joint proposal would streamline the process for reporting sexual misconduct allegations and make it easier for victims to report those allegations. It also would bar any House member from having an intimate relationship with any congressional staffer, building on an existing prohibition on members having relationships with their direct subordinates.

“Change happens when people are heard. The Ethics Committee was clearly listening to women staffers, and has been a great partner in our work,” said Leger Fernández in a statement Tuesday. She added that the panel reached out to the Democratic Women's Caucus, which she chairs, as it crafted its proposed new rules.

Cammack, who chairs the Republican Women's Caucus, said she plans to weigh in after the Ethics Committee votes on the changes Thursday.

item.title: Comer makes Kentucky governor bid official
item.description: The Republican House Oversight chair is looking to succeed Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear, who has led the red state since 2019.

media:content.media:title: Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.) departs a House Republican Conference leadership election on Capitol Hill on Nov. 10, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Ashley Ahn
item.content:encoded:
Republican Rep. James Comer announced he is running for governor of Kentucky next year, in a bid to flip the governorship from blue to red.

Comer has publicly floated his gubernatorial aspirations for months. He said in a virtual town hall Monday that he would focus on lowering taxes and expanding economic opportunities for the state.

“We got to make sure that people who are working hard and struggling can keep more of what they earn by reducing taxes,” he said.

Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear, who is term-limited, has led the deep-red state since 2019.

The long-previewed announcement comes weeks before Democrats take full control of Congress and are on track to amass their largest majority since the 2008 election. Seven House races and one Senate race have yet to be called.

Comer, who chairs the House Oversight Committee, led an investigation into Jeffrey Epstein last year that revealed thousands of documents shedding light on the late convicted sex offender’s relationships with several prominent figures, including President Donald Trump. He successfully forced former President Bill Clinton and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton to testify in his panel’s investigation, the first time a former president has been compelled to speak to Congress under subpoena.

Comer said in a statement last week that he would step down as the top Republican on the panel in January due to Republican Conference term limit rules.

item.title: Mike Johnson backs crackdown on House GOP holdouts
item.description: One proposal would have the Republican Steering Committee dole out consequences.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Mike Flood (R-Neb.) speaks with reporters as he departs a vote at the U.S. Capitol on Sept. 1, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Mia McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
Speaker Mike Johnson said Tuesday he supports an effort to create disciplinary rules for House Republicans who break with the party on certain procedural votes, adding new pressure on the incoming leaders to adopt the proposal ahead of the new Congress.

Johnson (R-La.) said he supported "a member-driven process” to develop standards around voting for "rules" — the procedural resolutions that set up debate on major bills headed to the House floor. As speaker, Johnson routinely dealt with holdout Republicans who used those votes to extract policy concessions.

The outgoing speaker noted “a lot of interest” in cracking down on those holdouts and said, “I support it.”

Johnson said he had to “deal with one of the smallest margins and a lot of disruptions” as speaker: “I think that frustrated members, and they want to have a remedy of that going forward."

There is no single proposal to regulate member conduct as of yet. One approach, pursued by the moderate Main Street Caucus, would empower the House GOP Steering Committee to determine punishments for maverick members.

Rep. Mike Flood (R-Neb.), the group's chair, said in an interview its members are consulting widely among leaders and the broader conference about the proposal. He said he is "open-minded" about the particulars and said some have suggested a supermajority vote of the steering panel be required to sanction a member.

"We had a lot of great successes in the 119th Congress, but we also had some hiccups," Flood said. "And most of the time there was a hiccup, it was tied to a very small number of members refusing to vote for a rule."

The Main Street proposal and other possible variants are set to come up for debate among House Republicans after they return from next week's Thanksgiving recess.

Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, the incoming GOP leader, said Tuesday, “We'll have a discussion in the conference.”

“Members are talking about all kinds of things,” he added, noting that Republicans are likely to be unified against the incoming Democratic majority: “This next two years, we're all going to be voting against the rules.”

item.title: Cory Booker wants to keep his leadership spot
item.description: The New Jersey Democrat is in charge of helping shape the caucus’ messaging and strategy.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) speaks with reporters at the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 16, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Jordain Carney
item.content:encoded:
New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker said in an interview Tuesday he wants to keep his current spot in the Senate Democratic leadership.

Booker is chair of the strategic communications committee, the No. 4 ranking spot. Underneath him is Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who is looking to move up the leadership ladder — possibly to the No. 3 steering and policy spot now held by outgoing Sen. Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota.

Booker said that he was “proud” of the messaging work he did during the 2026 cycle, including racking up “over a billion engagements” for the 47-member caucus on social media, and that “we can grow it significantly more now that we’ve got momentum.”

“I think we can only go bigger and bigger, and I want to continue doing that work,” he added. “I hope my colleagues appreciate the work that I’ve done.”

Booker's decision to stand pat comes amid a pitched fight over the No. 1 leader spot between Sens. Chuck Schumer of New York and Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, as well as the expected ascension of Sen. Brian Schatz of Hawaii to replace retiring Illinois Sen. Dick Durbin at No. 2.

Meanwhile, a down-ballot shuffle could be in the cards. Warren could choose to pursue the post now held by Klobuchar, given the liberal firebrand’s particular interest in policy matters. Democrats also view moderate Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada as another possible candidate amid speculation about splitting up the policy and steering portfolio.

item.title: Cruz announces partial deal on aviation safety overhaul
item.description: The Senate Commerce Committee chair said the agreement would mandate an aircraft location-receiving technology, though he acknowledged "we still have a couple of details to negotiate” related to the military.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) arrives for a vote at the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 16, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Sam Ogozalek
item.content:encoded:
Nearly two years after a deadly midair crash over Washington, Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz (R-Texas) said Tuesday that a partial deal had been reached on an air safety overhaul meant to avoid that calamity again.

Cruz said the Senate and House had "reached an agreement in principle" to mandate a type of location-receiving technology known as Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast In, or ADS-B In, on flights that already must broadcast via ADS-B Out.

He acknowledged that more work was to be done. "We still have a couple of details to negotiate with the House Armed Services Committee," he said at an event for victims' families outside the Capitol. "But with this agreement in principle, I believe we’re going to get this bill done, and my objective is to get it done this year.”

He added, "We are very, very close" on a broader deal.

It wasn't immediately clear what those details were nor was it clear what the ADS-B In deal entails exactly.

The breakthrough significantly increases the odds that Congress may finish the push to finalize air safety legislation during the lame-duck session of Congress.

Negotiators hope to have finalized text on the entire package by Thanksgiving, and it could move on the annual National Defense Authorization Act or as a standalone bill, said a person familiar with the matter, granted anonymity to speak candidly.

Committee ranking member Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) added that the agreement is on civil aviation provisions and that it was reached Thursday with the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.

ADS-B In language had been a major sticking point as the Senate and House championed competing bills responding to last year’s Washington midair disaster, the ROTOR Act, S. 2503 (119), and the ALERT Act, H.R. 7613 (119), respectively.

A spokesperson for the House Armed Services Committee didn’t immediately provide comment.

The January 2025 crash between a PSA Airlines jet and Army Black Hawk helicopter killed 67.

item.title: Jensen Huang agrees to testify on Capitol Hill
item.description: Nvidia’s top lawyer, Tim Teter, also agreed to testify.

media:content.media:title: Jensen Huang departs after a welcome ceremony with President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping at the Great Hall of the People on May 14, 2026, in Beijing.

item.dc:creator: By Owen Dahlkamp
item.content:encoded:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang will testify before three House committees on Dec. 1, three GOP lawmakers announced Tuesday.

Huang, who resigned after two affairs came to light, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, will appear before the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence and China Select committees for a transcribed interview. Lawmakers have expressed bipartisan concerns that China-based companies gained access to advanced semiconductor technology by leveraging Huang’s relationship with an executive at the computing company Megaspeed.

A spokesperson for Huang declined to comment.

The company’s general counsel, Tim Teter, will also appear for an interview on Dec. 2. “We look forward to meeting with the chairmen on Dec. 2,” a spokesperson for Nvidia said.

“The American people need answers on Mr. Huang and Nvidia’s role in allowing dangerous [People’s Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal,” the chairs of the three committees — Republican Reps. Brian Mast of Florida, John Moolenaar of Michigan and Rick Crawford of Arkansas — said in a statement.

The chairs sent letters to Huang and Teter on Thursday threatening to subpoena them if they did not voluntarily testify.

item.title: Democrats press Cruz to postpone FCC nominee’s vote
item.description: Senate Commerce Democrats want to move Republican and Democratic nominees together in the new Congress.

media:content.media:title: Senate Commerce Democrats want the committee to hold off on standalone consideration of a GOP nominee to the Federal Communications Commission.

item.dc:creator: By John Hendel
item.content:encoded:
The Senate Commerce Committee should scrap its plans to vote on Federal Communications Commission nominee Danielle Thumann Severs and skip any consideration during the lame duck, all Democratic members told Chair Ted Cruz (R-Texas) in a letter released Tuesday.

“There is no mandate for the outgoing majority to rush through a partisan FCC nomination in its final weeks,” wrote the Democrats, led by ranking member Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.).

Cruz, however, intends to proceed with Wednesday's markup agenda. "We look forward to reporting her out tomorrow and suggest Senate Democrats weigh in with the White House on nominating Democrats to the unfilled spot," said Senate Commerce Committee spokesperson Blair Taylor.

A White House spokesperson didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

President Donald Trump nominated Severs, an aide to FCC Chair Brendan Carr, to an open GOP seat on the five-member agency this summer. Her confirmation would give Carr a 3-1 majority, and critics fear Trump could use that opportunity to oust Anna Gomez, the lone Democrat.

Democrats’ letter said Severs’ nomination should not be considered until the next Congress, when Democrats control the chamber, and paired with Gomez’s renomination. Their letter noted that the president has recently nominated Democrats to other boards and argued a bipartisan approach to nominations has “served both parties.” Gomez’s holdover time in her seat expires at the end of next year.

Carr has drawn pushback from Democrats and some Republicans like Cruz for his threats to media companies and fights over broadcast licensing — concerns Democrats alluded to in their letter.

“At last week’s Committee hearing, Senate Democrats voiced concerns about Ms. Thumann Severs’s close relationship with FCC Chairman Carr and how that would impact her support for Chairman Carr’s controversial policies, some of which you have opposed as well,” the letter said.

item.title: Capitol agenda: No quick exit from Dem leader brawl
item.description: Interviews with about a dozen Democratic senators and senior aides revealed Monday there is little appetite for their majority leader election — now on tap for Dec. 1 — to be moved up to this week.

media:content.media:title: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer looks on during a press conference on AI at the U.S. Capitol on Sept. 23, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Calen Razor
item.content:encoded:
Senate Democrats may be settling in for a long and messy majority leader fight after Tuesday’s caucus lunch.

Interviews with about a dozen Democratic senators and senior aides revealed Monday there is little appetite for their majority leader election — now on tap for Dec. 1 — to be moved up to this week.

Expediting the closed-door vote had been floated by members eager to resolve the fight between Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Sen. Chris Van Hollen. Some privately express a desire to avoid being constantly pressed for public commitments in the race, and more wish to refocus on their governing agenda.

But members Monday appeared willing to tough it out for two more weeks.

“I would oppose expediting before we’ve had a full process,” said Sen. Jon Ossoff, who hasn’t backed a candidate.

The discussion will come to a head in the Senate Democratic lunch Tuesday — their first since Van Hollen threw his hat in the ring. A senator could call for a vote to waive caucus rules and hold the election sooner — though no one has publicly said they’ll do so. Schumer also has not called for the change, and Van Hollen has publicly opposed the move.

“It’s a family conversation that we’re going to have amongst ourselves,” Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester told reporters.

Moving up the vote would’ve been viewed as benefiting Schumer. While Schumer says he’s gathered the minimum 28 or 29 votes to win, only about 15 Democratic senators have publicly backed that support. Several others, granted anonymity to describe their intentions without courting public backlash, privately say they will support him.

Van Hollen has put his supporter count around 15, though his public endorsements so far remain in the single digits.

Otherwise, the public whip count has largely stagnated since last week — even as some senators praise the incumbent leader.

Sen. John Hickenlooper, for instance, made a coin-toss motion when asked who he’d support.

“Leave it to the Democrats that we flip nine seats, and the person who actually helps put it all together and do all that and all of a sudden, there’s a revolt,” he said, referring to Schumer.


What else we’re watching: 

— DUFFY’S $50B ASK GETS HILL REALITY CHECK — Senators are all but ruling out immediate approval of the Trump administration’s $50 billion request to overhaul the nation’s air traffic control system. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy will be on Capitol Hill Tuesday to make his case to Republicans at their regular GOP weekly lunch following last week’s hourslong ground stop due to a malfunction of aviation communication infrastructure. Senate Majority Leader John Thune on Monday shot down the idea of muscling the money through Congress using a GOP-only reconciliation bill — instead raising the prospect of negotiating the funding with Democrats.
 
— GOP BALKS AT TALK OF HUANG RETURN — GOP lawmakers were wary of the suggestion that Jensen Huang should return to chipmaker Nvidia, despite Trump’s defense of the company’s former CEO. Nine GOP lawmakers, including members of Senate Banking and Foreign Affairs, rebuffed the suggestion that Huang should return following his ouster last week amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy. Lawmakers also rejected pressure from powerful tech leaders who pushed for his reinstatement and a suggestion from the president that he’s learned his lesson. The comments from senior Republicans mark an emphatic break with Trump, who has maintained a close relationship with Huang.

Jordain Carney, Sam Ogozalek, Samuel Larreal, Katherine Long and Ari Hawkins contributed to this report.

item.title: Senate Democrats reject quick exit from Schumer vs. Van Hollen fight
item.description: A Tuesday caucus lunch will be just the beginning of a “family conversation” about the contentious race, senators say.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) speaks with reporters as he arrives for a vote at the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 16, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Jordain Carney
item.content:encoded:
Senate Democrats are preparing for their all-consuming fight over who will lead them next year to drag on for weeks.

The contentious battle between Sens. Chuck Schumer of New York and Chris Van Hollen of Maryland has already become, in the minds of some Democrats, a massive distraction from the work of preparing for a new majority and looming battles with President Donald Trump.

But interviews with about a dozen Democratic senators and senior aides Monday revealed little appetite to end the drama this week by moving up the closed-door election currently scheduled for Dec. 1.

“I would oppose expediting before we’ve had a full process,” said Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), who hasn’t backed a candidate.

Sen. John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.), who is also publicly uncommitted, said, “I don’t think that’s going to happen.”

Moving up the vote would have been viewed as benefiting Schumer, the longtime top Democrat who said last week he had secured the votes for a second stint as majority leader. But Schumer has not called for changing the schedule, and Van Hollen is publicly opposed to any such move.

Given that, and the uproar among many Democratic voters unhappy with Schumer’s recent leadership, senators appear willing to tough it out for two more weeks. They include Schumer allies, Van Hollen diehards and the dozens of publicly undecided Senate Democrats — even as some privately express a desire to avoid being constantly pressed for public commitments in the race, and many more wish to refocus on their governing agenda.

Tuesday’s caucus lunch is the first time Senate Democrats will gather in person since Van Hollen announced his leadership bid Thursday night. A senator could use the opportunity to call for a vote to waive caucus rules and hold the election later this week. Instead, some Democrats said Tuesday they were simply hoping for a robust discussion.

“It’s a family conversation that we’re going to have amongst ourselves,” said Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.).

Van Hollen has been waging an unusually public campaign for leader that began with a cable-TV interview Thursday and has since expanded to include a “Chris for Leader” website and multiple Sunday talk show interviews. In an interview with POLITICO Sunday, he not only called for new leadership but also openly criticized Schumer’s record — pointing out, for instance, his opposition to the 2015 Iran nuclear deal that Trump later tore up.

“I’m really worried that we might blow what could be a huge opportunity to deliver,” Van Hollen said Monday, adding that he believes he has “momentum” in his supporter count.

Schumer, meanwhile, has focused almost solely on talking privately with colleagues since late last week — sticking to the traditional approach to a race that will be decided on a secret ballot of the 55 or 56 Democratic senators set to be sworn in early next year. He’s still viewed as the favorite due to the relationships he has built, funds he has raised and victories the party notched in this month’s midterms.

“I have a long history with Chuck,” said Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii), who became the latest senator to publicly back Schumer Monday.

But scores of Senate Democrats are staying quiet. Coming out in support of Schumer would only put a target on their backs with some Democratic activists, who are ramping up an external pressure campaign on behalf of Van Hollen and remain furious over Schumer’s decision early in Trump’s second term to advance a GOP funding bill as well as his reluctance to cut off U.S. aid to Israel, among other issues.

While Schumer says he’s gathered the minimum 28 or 29 votes to win, only about 15 have publicly backed that support. Several others, granted anonymity to describe their intentions without courting public backlash, privately say they will support him. Van Hollen, meanwhile, has put his supporter count around 15, though his public endorsements so far remain in the single digits.

Otherwise, the public whip count has largely stagnated after an initial round of endorsements after Van Hollen jumped in last week — even as some senators conspicuously praise the incumbent leader.

Hickenlooper, for instance, made a coin-toss motion when asked who he was supporting. But he appeared to question why some Democrats were trying to ditch Schumer after they just outperformed even the rosiest election projections.

“Leave it to the Democrats that we flip nine seats, and the person who actually helps put it all together and do all that and all of a sudden, there's a revolt,” he said.

Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.) also said he was undecided before listing Schumer’s assets: “Chuck delivered an amazing win. Chuck knows Trump, and that'll be really really important going forward.”

“No one, who is not on the ballot, worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer,” Kaine said before adding a third consideration: “Voters are demanding change.”

Several other veteran senators declined to state their voting intentions Monday. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), who is expected to become Banking chair and is looking to move up the leadership ladder, did not respond to questions from reporters in the halls. Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.), another member of leadership and a potential 2028 contender, used the same terms as Blunt Rochester, calling the matter a “family conversation.”

Sen. Michael Bennet (D-Colo.), who stopped just short of calling on Schumer to resign last year, dodged questions from reporters, while Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), who has been critical of Schumer and the DSCC’s approach to primaries, also said Monday he is in listening mode.

“I’m going to hear them both out, and I want to hear from the freshman class as well,” he said.

Katherine Tully-McManus and Calen Razor contributed to this report.

item.title: Ron Johnson holds out hope for 'relatively simple' GOP spending bill
item.description: The Senate Budget chair said he believed a new reconciliation package could start moving this week.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.) pushes a button for an elevator as he is pursued by reporters after a vote at the U.S. Capitol on July 13, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Mia McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
Senate Budget Chair Ron Johnson said he believed Republicans could pave the way for a final party-line spending bill before Democrats take control on Capitol Hill by putting a fiscal blueprint up for a vote later this week.

“I think what we're probably looking at is a relatively simple package that makes it pretty easy,” the Wisconsin Republican said. “I would hope we could pass a resolution this week.”

Johnson was noncommittal on the details — including whether it would include the $350 billion in defense funding that President Donald Trump called for last week — and reiterated that the committee is working through the details.

Asked about the possibility of a budget vote this week, Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said, "We'll see."

House Republicans sent the Senate a budget resolution that would unlock the party-line reconciliation process in July. It included only $74 billion in military funding in addition to farm aid and election integrity spending and has not advanced in the Senate.

Trump’s defense ask, Johnson said, “simplified the process,” but he acknowledged ongoing talks about possibly adding a debt ceiling hike to the proposal. Thune said "it’s obviously whatever we can get 50" votes to pass.

Pressed on when he might release text of a budget resolution, Johnson said, “Text is easy.”

The hard part, he added, is “deciding what can pass."

Jordain Carney contributed to this report.

item.title: Trump nominates top White House aide to head watchdog agency — as Democrats feared
item.description: The president has nominated Eric Ueland to head the Government Accountability Office.

media:content.media:title: Eric Ueland, President Donald Trump's pick to be deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget, appearing before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on Thursday.

item.dc:creator: By Katherine Tully-McManus, Jennifer Scholtes and Calen Razor
item.dc:contributor: By Katherine Tully-McManus, Jennifer Scholtes and Calen Razor
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump has nominated Eric Ueland as comptroller general and head of the Government Accountability Office, a position empowered to sue the administration on Congress’ behalf.

It marks the president’s last-ditch effort to get one of his allies confirmed to the post before Democrats take control of Congress in January. It also comes as lawmakers in both parties are calling for the independent oversight agency to challenge the Trump administration before the Supreme Court for withholding federal cash Congress has approved.

Ueland is currently the deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget, which is at the forefront of efforts to withhold and cancel federal funding. That makes him a pariah among Democrats who have already criticized Republicans of facilitating a “sham” confirmation process that breaks precedent for how the comptroller general is typically nominated.

And even though Ueland is generally popular among Republicans, his confirmation is not guaranteed. Some Senate Republicans are questioning whether it’s appropriate to confirm a sitting executive branch official to a position responsible for investigating and challenging the moves of that same administration.

“I think Eric's a really qualified individual, but I have concerns that this is the partisan pick for a very bipartisan office,” Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) said in an interview Monday. “He's very qualified, but I think there's some strong partisan leanings on his part.”

The Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee will hold a hearing on his nomination Thursday — and the panel’s chair, Sen. Rand Paul, held off on a public endorsement Monday night.

“I stick with what I said last year about it. I think it's important to find someone who's honest and objective,” the Kentucky Republican said in a brief interview.

Paul then told reporters that the White House asked him to put Ueland’s name forward for the role. And asked if he pushed back on the administration, he said: “That's all I've got for you.”

Ueland is a known entity on Capitol Hill: He was a longtime Senate aide who spent time as staff director for Senate Budget Committee Republicans under then-Chair Michael Enzi of Wyoming, and was chief of staff to former Republican Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist.

He was also the White House director of legislative affairs during the first Trump administration, when he brokered talks on Capitol Hill between then-Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin and senators to build an economic relief package that could clear the Senate as the Covid-19 pandemic bore down on U.S. markets.

Sen. James Lankford (R-Okla.) said Ueland is “seen as a straightforward, fair person that understands the operation of government and of agencies.”

“He's done so many different roles in so many different places,” Lankford said in an interview Monday, adding that he met with Ueland in his office a few months ago. “He has a good perspective of multiple agencies, and so I know where he's coming from.”

Still, Democrats and some Republicans have been eager for the agency to take the administration to court — something that could be politically difficult for someone in Ueland’s position to execute, given his relationships with top White House officials.

The agency, which has been operating under an acting comptroller general since last December, has issued more than a half-dozen findings of illegal impoundment of federal dollars since the start of Trump’s second term.

But so far, it has not taken legal action — even though the Supreme Court suggested last fall that GAO is the only entity with standing to sue the Trump administration for violating the decades-old Impoundment Control Act, which was designed to ensure presidents spend money Congress approves and exactly as lawmakers intended.

item.title: Phillip Swagel, longtime CBO director, will retire in January
item.description: Incoming Democratic leaders will get to select a replacement for nonpartisan fiscal scorekeeper.

media:content.media:title: Phillip Swagel, director of the Congressional Budget Office, testifies during a House committee hearing on the CBO's budget and economic outlook Feb. 14, 2024, on Capitol Hill in Washington.

item.dc:creator: By Katherine Tully-McManus
item.content:encoded:
Phillip Swagel, the longtime head of Congress’ nonpartisan scorekeeping agency, will leave Capitol Hill when his term is up in January, he said Monday.

His exit sets up a big decision for the Democratic leaders of the incoming Congress. Chairs of the House and Senate Budget committees are responsible for recommending a candidate for leading the agency, whom congressional leaders then appoint. That is expected to put Rep. Brendan Boyle (D-Pa.) and Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.) in charge of considering potential candidates.

Swagel, who has led the Congressional Budget Office since 2019, plans to return to academia and resume teaching economics at the University of Maryland. Swagel previously served as an assistant Treasury secretary under former President George W. Bush.

Swagel thanked past and present chairs and ranking members of the House and Senate Budget committees “for their support and guidance” during his term in his farewell message.

“I appreciate the many Members of Congress and staff who have relied on CBO to help inform their efforts on behalf of the nation,” Swagel said. “The time I have spent with Members has deepened my respect for their knowledge, thoughtfulness, and commitment to the people they represent.”

Swagel has maintained a productive relationship with GOP lawmakers in recent years despite their balking over the more than $4 trillion price tag he projected for the domestic policy megabill Republicans enacted last year.

The budget director accommodated the GOP’s decision to employ a controversial accounting tactic to estimate the cost of that bill, providing lawmakers with alternate projections that allowed them to claim the legislation would cost far less than under the traditional method — and sidestepped procedural headaches in the Senate.

Swagel this year also helped Republican lawmakers in their search for ways to root out “waste, fraud and abuse” in federal programs. The nonpartisan budget office worked with the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to pinpoint cost-cutting policy changes, including spending money to crack down on fraud in payments to providers of skin substitutes.

Swagel’s office at CBO features a stuffed skunk, a gift from staff nodding to a long-running joke about CBO’s role as a voice of fiscal reality — the skunk at the legislative garden party.

Jennifer Scholtes contributed to this report.

item.title: Duffy, Bedford huddle with Congress following air system meltdown
item.description: The FAA chief briefed lawmakers Sunday; the Transportation secretary will be on the Hill Tuesday. "Key" members of government will meet at the White House today.

media:content.media:title: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy (right), with Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford at a news conference Saturday following a nationwide ground stop.

item.dc:creator: By Oriana Pawlyk
item.content:encoded:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford and other government officials are fanning out to brief Congress and the White House on Friday’s nationwide air system meltdown that led to a multihour ground stop.

Bedford held a virtual meeting with House and Senate members Sunday, while Duffy intends to speak to lawmakers at the Republican lunch Tuesday, according to a person familiar with the leaders’ fluid schedules, granted anonymity to speak candidly.

On Monday, Democrats on the House Transportation Committee, led by ranking member Rick Larsen (D-Wash.) said that committee staff will meet virtually on Tuesday with FAA and DOT officials for a briefing.

Separately, “key members of government” will be at the White House on Monday to discuss the ground stop and “how to prevent this situation from ever happening again,” a White House official said Monday and granted anonymity to discuss the planning.

Duffy is not expected to attend, the person said.

Duffy has spent months pitching the need for a new air traffic control system and previously told POLITICO he planned to head to Capitol Hill this week to lobby Congress for more funding for the “Brand New Air Traffic Control System,” the FAA’s long-sought modernization effort.

However, since the meltdown, Duffy has upped his ask from $30 billion to $50 billion. Duffy, who made the rounds on several Sunday talk shows, said it was still unclear whether Friday’s error happened due to incompetence or faulty equipment. The monthslong work is being done by L3Harris, a longtime contractor for the Federal Aviation Administration. The contractor is working to switch communications systems to fiber from the aging copper wire that serves dozens of facilities.

“We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel,” L3Harris said in a statement Saturday, adding it “takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.”

Alex Gangitano contributed to this report.

item.title: Capitol agenda: Van Hollen takes the inside game outside
item.description: The Maryland senator’s outside pressure playbook could rally many in the party’s base and provide a template for what leadership bids become in the future.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Chris Van Hollen speaks during the Senate Subcommittee on Commerce, Justice, Science and Related Agencies hearing on Capitol Hill, May 12, 2026, in Washington.

item.dc:creator: By Calen Razor
item.content:encoded:
Chris Van Hollen may not ultimately win Senate majority leader, but he’s running a leadership race unlike any seen before.

Rather than focusing solely on the inside game of winning over his colleagues, the Maryland senator is mounting a very public bid against Minority Leader Chuck Schumer — forcing the Democratic caucus beyond private deliberations into a messy debate about their future.

The Maryland senator’s outside pressure playbook could rally many in the party’s base and transform the way these races are fought — and provide a template for what leadership bids become in the future.

His first test of success could come as soon as the party lunch Tuesday afternoon, when the discussion on whether or not to waive caucus rules and move up the leadership election to this week from Dec. 1 could come to a head.

Van Hollen told POLITICO Playbook in an interview Sunday he believes there’s enough support within the caucus to prevent the secret ballot election from happening this week. Schumer hasn’t yet weighed in on the idea.

“I think that there’s an overwhelming sentiment that we should have a fair and open process,” Van Hollen said. “I guess I would just ask why it would be that folks want to cut debate short. Is it because the longer this discussion goes on, the more our momentum grows?”

Van Hollen has otherwise been on a media run since announcing his bid against Schumer, including defending his “underdog” challenge while delivering remarks at Democrats’ “What’s Next” conference in Denver, Colorado.

He also launched a website over the weekend where supporters of his leadership bid submit their names and emails — a move that privately made some senators question whether his leadership challenge is a backdoor way to build up a 2028 presidential bid.

The email list, Van Hollen told Playbook, “is a way to get an early start for our Senate candidates in 2028. … The website allows people to contribute to the candidates.”

Schumer, meanwhile, continues to play the inside game after insisting he has the votes to win leader — even as some Democratic aides privately say they wish he’d mount a firmer public defense of himself. He’s still viewed as the favorite.

Among his backers are some senators who don’t like Van Hollen’s penchant for criticizing the party, according to two people granted anonymity to disclose private thinking.
